background.definition: Having a rough, harsh, weak, or breathy voice. Often synonymous with dysphonia.

list.listitem: Laryngeal cancer incidence 3.6 per 100,000 in the United States.
Laryngeal cancer prevalence 93,096 in the United States in 2005.
Neoplasm (e.g. squamous cell, lymphoma, and sarcoma).
Benign vocal fold masses (polyps, cysts, and nodules).
Vocal fold paresis or paralysis.
Systemic neurological disorders (ALS, myasthenia gravis, Parkinson's, and CVA).
Systemic disease (rheumatoid arthritis, sarcoidosis, and amyloidosis).
Cervical trauma.
Recurrent respiratory papilloma (RRP).
Extraesophageal reflux or laryngopharyngeal reflux (LPR; an entity distinct from GERD).
Respiratory infection.
Presbyphonia (vocal changes in the aging larynx).
Iatrogenic (prolonged intubation, s/p thyroidectomy, or spine surgery).
Inhaled corticosteroids, especially at higher doses.
Hoarseness is a diagnosis and a symptom or description of voice quality. Pathophysiology is dependent on the underlying etiology.
Hoarseness results from abnormal vocal fold mobility, incomplete glottic closure, or inability of the vocal folds to vibrate normally as a result of edema or mass effect.
Avoid risk factors such as tobacco and alcohol, and if present adequately treat gastroesophageal reflux disease, allergies, and sinus infection. C
Adequate hydration and avoiding vocal overuse or misuse (eg, shouting, chronic throat-clearing) are preventive options. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Chronic, progressive, associated with dysphagia or otalgia, weight loss, fatigue, and neck mass
Acute, recent URI, fever, usually viral and self-limiting

Differential.Differential_Name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) or laryngopharyngeal reflux (LPR)
Differential.Differential_Features: Worse in AM, associated globus, throat clearing, excessive mucus
Professional voice users (singers, teachers, and telemarketers)
Recent surgery (cervical fusion, thyroidectomy, skull-base surgery, and CABG)
Breathy, weak voice, may follow recent URI, persists, and signs of aspiration

list.listitem: Patients will present with altered voice (weak, breathy, strained, raspy, and absent). In a study of patients referred for hoarseness, 12% were ultimately diagnosed with cancer.
Onset and duration are important for the differential diagnosis.
Ask about associated symptoms worrisome for malignancy: painful or difficult swallowing, ear pain, hemoptysis, and weight loss.
Physical examination is usually normal. Associated cervical lymphadenopathy is concerning for malignancy.
Improvement after empiric treatment of GERD or laryngopharyngeal reflux with twice daily PPI supports the diagnosis.
Persistent, worsening hoarseness associated with constitutional symptoms, otalgia, dysphagia, hemoptysis, or neck masses is highly suggestive of malignancy.

Fiberoptic laryngoscopy is the key to diagnosing most causes of hoarseness. It is recommended for any patient with symptoms persisting more than a maximum of 3 months. Some clinicians recommend earlier referral, i.e. after 2 weeks of hoarseness, although clinical trials are lacking.

Laryngoscopy with biopsy establishes the diagnosis for suspected laryngeal neoplasms, benign nodules, recurrent respiratory papilloma, or systemic diseases. Laryngeal stroboscopy gives the appearance of vocal fold mobility in slow motion and is useful for diagnosing subtle pathology.
Laboratory blood tests are of low yield unless there is suspicion of a systemic process.

Order CXR if suspected pulmonary disease (asthma, bronchitis, and lung cancer). Order CT of neck with contrast for patients presenting with concomitant cervical adenopathy or neck masses. CT or MRI are not routinely recommended prior to laryngoscopy.
Fine-needle aspiration of cervical lymph nodes/masses is high yield and can often make the diagnosis.

Diagnosis of laryngopharyngeal reflux (LPR) is less definitive and is based on history, symptoms, laryngoscopic appearance, and adjunctive studies. Dual-channel pH probe testing (ambulatory 24-hour probes placed in the lower esophagus and pharynx) is a valuable diagnostic test in suspected extraesophageal reflux or LPR.
